group.title: Rhetoric and politics
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A leader who wins support by stirring up people’s fears and prejudices.
examples: The {demagogue} blamed outsiders for every problem.
wrong: A demagogue calmly explains complex facts and never plays on emotion.

words.meaning: A strong written or spoken attack on an idea or person.
examples: Her book is a fierce {polemic} against waste.
wrong: His polemic gently praised every side of the debate.

words.meaning: Very insulting and angry language.
examples: He launched into a stream of {invective}.
wrong: Her invective was full of kind and gentle praise.

words.meaning: Deliberate exaggeration for effect.
examples: Saying he’s "the greatest player in history" is {hyperbole}.
wrong: "It was fairly nice" is a perfect example of hyperbole.

words.meaning: A question asked for effect, not to get an answer.
examples: "Who doesn’t want to be happy?" is a {rhetorical question}.
wrong: She asked a rhetorical question and waited for a detailed reply.

words.meaning: Attacking the person rather than their argument.
examples: Calling him lazy was an {ad hominem} attack, not a reply.
wrong: His ad hominem reply focused only on the facts of the argument.

words.meaning: Something that draws attention away from the real issue.
examples: The talk about his tie was a {red herring}.
wrong: The red herring kept everyone focused on the main issue.

words.meaning: A short, catchy phrase from a speech, used in the news.
examples: The campaign relies on {soundbites} rather than policy.
wrong: A soundbite is a long, detailed policy document.

words.meaning: To redraw voting areas unfairly so one party gains an advantage.
examples: Critics say the party {gerrymandered} the districts to keep power.
wrong: They gerrymandered the map to give both parties a fairer chance.

words.meaning: A very long speech made to delay or block a vote.
examples: The senator’s {filibuster} lasted fifteen hours.
wrong: A filibuster is a quick vote that ends a debate at once.

words.meaning: Supported by two opposing political parties.
examples: The bill passed with {bipartisan} support.
wrong: The bipartisan plan was backed by only one party.

words.meaning: Extreme, aggressive pride in your country, often in favor of war.
examples: The war was fueled by newspaper {jingoism}.
wrong: His jingoism made him call for peace and friendship with every nation.

words.meaning: Government by a small, powerful group.
examples: The country is ruled by a wealthy {oligarchy}.
wrong: An oligarchy gives equal power to every citizen.

words.meaning: Government by the rich.
examples: Critics warn that money is turning democracy into {plutocracy}.
wrong: In a plutocracy, the poorest people hold all the power.

words.meaning: Government by one person with total power.
examples: The country slid from democracy into {autocracy}.
wrong: In an autocracy, power is shared among many elected bodies.

words.meaning: Politics that claims to speak for ordinary people against a powerful elite.
examples: A wave of {populism} swept the election.
wrong: Populism is politics that openly speaks only for the elite.

words.meaning: A skilled public speaker.
examples: She was a gifted {orator} who held crowds spellbound.
wrong: As an orator, he was too shy to ever speak in public.

words.meaning: To lecture someone loudly and at length, often angrily.
examples: The coach {harangued} the team at halftime.
wrong: He harangued us with a short, quiet word of praise.

words.meaning: To strongly urge someone to do something.
examples: The leader {exhorted} citizens to stay calm.
wrong: She exhorted them to act by telling them to do nothing.

words.meaning: To persuade someone gently, with flattery or promises.
examples: She {cajoled} him into giving a speech.
wrong: He cajoled her by shouting threats and orders.

words.meaning: The person who currently holds an official position.
examples: The {incumbent} won a third term.
wrong: The incumbent is a newcomer who has never held the office.

words.meaning: All the people who can vote in an election.
examples: The {electorate} is tired of broken promises.
wrong: The electorate is the small group of candidates running for office.

words.meaning: The voters in an area represented by one official; a group of supporters.
examples: She visits her {constituency} every weekend.
wrong: A constituency is a politician’s private holiday home.

words.meaning: To take away someone’s right to vote or their power.
examples: The new rules could {disenfranchise} thousands of voters.
wrong: The law disenfranchised them by giving them the vote.

words.meaning: A person who openly opposes a government or official policy.
examples: The {dissident} was sent into exile.
wrong: A dissident is someone who loyally supports every government rule.

words.meaning: Speech or actions that encourage people to rebel against a government.
examples: The journalist was charged with {sedition}.
wrong: Sedition means urging people to obey and support the government.

words.meaning: Politics based on practical power and interests rather than ideals.
examples: The alliance was pure {realpolitik}.
wrong: Realpolitik puts moral ideals above any practical interest.

words.meaning: The people of a nation thought of as one political group.
examples: Corruption weakens the whole {body politic}.
wrong: The body politic is a single politician’s physical health.

words.meaning: To please a group by telling them what they want to hear.
examples: The candidate {pandered} to every crowd he met.
wrong: He pandered to the voters by telling them truths they hated.

words.meaning: To act in a showy way to win attention or praise.
examples: Senators {grandstanded} for the cameras.
wrong: She grandstanded by working quietly where no one could see.

words.meaning: A coded message meant to be understood only by a particular group.
examples: Critics called the slogan a {dog whistle}.
wrong: A dog whistle is a message everyone understands in the same way.

words.meaning: A prepared argument or phrase that people repeat to support a position.
examples: Every spokesperson repeated the same {talking point}.
wrong: A talking point is a remark made up on the spot by chance.

words.meaning: Grand, showy language that has little real meaning.
examples: His speech was all {bombast} and no substance.
wrong: Her bombast was plain, modest and full of facts.

words.meaning: Repeating the same words at the start of several phrases for effect.
examples: "Every child, every parent, every teacher" is a simple use of {anaphora}.
wrong: Anaphora means never repeating any word in a speech.

words.meaning: A speaker’s appeal to their own trustworthiness; also the spirit of a group.
examples: The doctor’s {ethos} made the audience believe her advice.
wrong: His ethos came from the fact that nobody trusted him.

words.meaning: The quality that stirs pity or emotion; an appeal to feelings.
examples: The speech relied on {pathos} rather than facts.
wrong: Her pathos left the audience cold and unmoved.

words.meaning: A person who argues in defense of something others criticize.
examples: He became an {apologist} for the government’s harsh policies.
wrong: As an apologist for the plan, she attacked it at every chance.

words.meaning: Strongly supporting one party or side, often unfairly.
examples: The debate became bitterly {partisan}.
wrong: Her partisan view was fair and balanced toward all sides.

words.meaning: Someone whose job is to present news in the best possible light for a politician.
examples: A {spin doctor} rewrote the minister’s statement.
wrong: A spin doctor reports bad news in the most damaging way possible.

words.meaning: The final part of a speech, meant to inspire the audience.
examples: Her {peroration} brought the crowd to its feet.
wrong: The peroration is the opening line of a speech.
